subject: Oil hit $113 while bond yields fell 19 basis points
bodyMarkdown:
If you are choosing between a fixed and a variable mortgage before the Bank of Canada decides on Wednesday, Thursday afternoon handed you two signals that point opposite ways. Oil closed at a five-month high, and the bond market that sets your fixed rate had its best day in more than three years.

## Oil moved on a newspaper story

CNBC reported on Thursday that Brent crude rose 4 per cent to close at US$113.17 a barrel, its highest close since May, after Trump hinted at renewed action against Iran. The trigger, according to that coverage, was a New York Times report that the United States and Israel have drawn up plans for fresh attacks on Iran after the midterm elections on November 3. Nothing has been hit yet. A plan got described in a newspaper and crude jumped 4 per cent, which tells you how little spare supply traders think is sitting around. Tiff Macklem told reporters earlier this month that if oil stays around US$100, he expects inflation to gradually drift up from 3 per cent. Oil is nowhere near US$100 now, and Statistics Canada's September CPI, out on Monday, already had gasoline up 27.8 per cent from a year earlier.

## The bond market went the other way

The same afternoon, the Globe and Mail reported that US Treasury yields plunged as worries about the AI boom's sustainability flared up again. The 10-year finished at 4.952 per cent, down 19.3 **basis points**, each one a hundredth of a percentage point, which was its sharpest one-day fall since March 2023. The 30-year closed at 5.286 per cent. None of that was about oil. Investors spent the day deciding that Meta's data centre plans mean more borrowing to pay for AI, sold the stocks and bought government bonds with the proceeds, and bets on further Fed hikes began to unwind. By Friday morning the 10-year had drifted back up to roughly 4.98 per cent, so a good chunk of Thursday was traders covering positions rather than a considered call on growth. Fixed mortgage rates here track the five-year Government of Canada yield, and that yield moves on weeks like this one.

## Canada took it from both sides

Reuters reported on Thursday that the S&P/TSX Composite fell 351.54 points, or 1 per cent, to 35,973.45. The sector breakdown is the odd part. Energy lost 1.7 per cent on a day when US crude settled 2.4 per cent higher at $99.47 a barrel, materials dropped 5.6 per cent to its lowest close since August 4, and technology fell 1.6 per cent, with Toronto's Celestica down about 12 per cent. So the oil price raised the cost of filling a tank in Richmond Hill without paying Canadians back through the energy stocks that usually cushion that. Macklem now goes into October 28 with the policy rate at 2.25 per cent, an oil shock lifting inflation expectations and a growth scare pulling long yields down.

## The takeaway

I still read Wednesday as a hold, and Thursday made the statement much harder to write than the decision. If you want a fixed rate, watch the five-year Government of Canada yield early next week and get a rate hold while the bond rally is still in the price, because lenders pass these moves on slowly going down and quickly going up. The number I am watching is Brent rather than the next CPI print, since every week crude stays above US$110 makes Macklem's drift-up warning more real. And if you own Canadian energy stocks as an inflation hedge, Thursday was a reminder that the hedge can fail on the exact day the inflation shows up.
